name: Al Reem Biosphere Reserve
blurb: Rain-fed gravel desert where oryx, gazelles and sand cats share thin pickings.

tip.title: Skip the rains
tip.text: Rain wakes the desert grasses and shrubs. Cut Desert bunch grasses by 100% and watch the oryx, the beetles and desert larks, then the shrikes, monitors and cats that feed on them.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Sunlight and heat
nodes.desc: Intense sun powers sparse plant growth, and daytime heat sends many animals into burrows or shade.

nodes.name: Rare winter rain
nodes.desc: Rain is scarce and irregular. After a shower, desert plants leaf out quickly and herds can follow the new growth.

nodes.name: Rainwater depressions (rawdat)
nodes.desc: Shallow depressions called rawdat collect rainwater and hold richer plant life than the surrounding rocky desert.

nodes.name: Thin desert soil
nodes.desc: Weathered, nutrient-poor gravel and sand soil that limits how much vegetation the desert can carry.

nodes.name: Bacteria and fungi
nodes.desc: Break down dead plants and animals, returning scarce nutrients to the soil.

nodes.name: Desert bunch grasses
nodes.desc: Grasses of sandy desert that green up after rain. Related Stipagrostis grasses are the main food of Arabian oryx in Oman.

nodes.name: Samr acacia
nodes.desc: A drought-tolerant thorny tree, among the most common plants in Qatar. Its pods and foliage are used as desert fodder and it fixes nitrogen in the soil.

nodes.name: Arfaj
nodes.desc: A yellow-flowered shrub native to Qatar, regarded as a main desert forage plant for camels and sheep. It leafs out quickly after rain.

nodes.name: Arabian oryx
nodes.desc: Mostly a grass eater that follows rains to fresh growth and can go weeks without water. Semi-managed herds live in Qatar.

nodes.name: Arabian sand gazelle
nodes.desc: The rheem, the native gazelle of Qatar. Gazelles of the Arabian peninsula browse mainly acacia and other woody plants.

nodes.name: Egyptian mastigure
nodes.desc: A large spiny-tailed lizard of open, gravelly desert. It shelters in burrows and feeds mainly on plants and seeds.

nodes.name: Pitted beetle
nodes.desc: A darkling beetle of arid Middle Eastern habitats, recorded in the Al Reem area. It is food for lizards, birds and shrikes.

nodes.name: Desert lark
nodes.desc: Eats seeds and insects, with more insects in the breeding season. A common small bird that predators of the desert hunt.

nodes.name: Blanford's short-nosed desert lizard
nodes.desc: A small desert lizard recorded in the area. It feeds on small invertebrates and is prey for wheatears, shrikes and monitors.

nodes.name: Desert wheatear
nodes.desc: An insectivore that picks ants, beetles and other insects from the ground. GloBI records show it eating small lizards too.

nodes.name: Great grey shrike
nodes.desc: A perch-and-pounce predator of rodents, songbirds, lizards and large insects, which it impales on thorns.

nodes.name: Arabian horned viper
nodes.desc: A sand-dwelling viper whose diet is thought to be mainly rodents, with beetles and lizards as smaller prey.

nodes.name: Desert monitor
nodes.desc: A burrowing carnivore that eats small mammals, reptiles, birds, eggs and insects, and also scavenges carrion.

nodes.name: Sand cat
nodes.desc: A small desert cat that hunts at night for rodents and birds, and also kills lizards and venomous snakes. It gets most of its water from prey.

nodes.name: Red fox
nodes.desc: An omnivore that takes small animals, birds, reptiles and insects, and eats carrion. Qatar has two fox species.
